# Cloud GPU Pricing Compared

What AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, RunPod, Lambda and CloudRift charge per GPU-hour, read from each provider's own price sheet and divided down to the single card. On demand, Linux, US regions, no commitment.

Provider prices read October 15, 2026. CloudRift column live, read November 14, 2026 at 2:38 PM UTC.

An hourly rate says little until you know what the card does in that hour. These are the published benchmarks behind the comparisons above, with the pricing basis each one used. We have no V100 or MI350X benchmark yet, so those rows stand on price alone.

## What the List Price Leaves Out

Why two honest comparisons of the same GPU can disagree by a factor of two.

Commitments

Google's 8-GPU H100 a3-megagpu-8g is $93.40 an hour on demand, $64.21 with a one-year commitment and $40.65 with three. AWS and Azure sell the same kind of one- and three-year terms.

Shapes You Cannot Buy on Demand

Google sells the B200 only through its Dynamic Workload Scheduler, and its single-GPU H100 shapes have left the on-demand list. At the hyperscalers the eight-GPU box is increasingly the unit.

Spot and Preemptible Rates

Google's spot price for that same 8-GPU H100 shape was $50.44 an hour on the day we read it. Spot capacity can be taken back at any time, so it suits batch work, not serving.

The Bundle Around the GPU

A hyperscaler GPU price buys a fixed set of vCPUs, memory and local disk with it. Google's attachable V100 and T4 prices exclude the N1 virtual machine they attach to, so the real hourly bill is higher.

Egress and Minimums

The hyperscalers bill data leaving the region per gigabyte on top of the GPU. CloudRift bills per second of runtime, with no minimum spend and no egress charges.

...

How much does an H100 cost per hour on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud?

On October 15, 2026: $6.88 per GPU-hour on AWS (p5.48xlarge, us-east-1), $12.29 on Azure (ND96isr_H100_v5, East US) and $11.06 on Google Cloud (a3-highgpu-8g, Iowa), all on demand for the eight-GPU shape. Azure's single H100 NVL shape is $6.98. RunPod and Lambda list the H100 SXM at $3.99.

What is the cheapest cloud GPU?

Among the providers on this page, the V100 on CloudRift at $0.25 per GPU-hour, below the hyperscalers’ T4 at $0.35 to $0.53. For current-generation cards, the RTX 4090 at $0.39 and the RTX 5090 at $0.65 on CloudRift, or RunPod’s community tier, which lists the same cards from $0.34 and $0.69 on shared hosts.

Why do GPU prices differ so much between providers?

The hyperscalers fold networking, storage, support and committed-use discounts into a higher list price and sell most accelerators in eight-GPU units. Specialist clouds run leaner, buy consumer and workstation cards the hyperscalers do not stock, and price per GPU. The same H100 ranges from $3.99 to $12.29 per hour on this page.

Are these prices on demand, and in which region?

Yes. Every number is the pay-as-you-go Linux price with no commitment: AWS us-east-1, Azure East US (East US 2 for the H200 and MI300X, which East US does not sell), Google Cloud us-central1. Spot, reserved and committed-use rates are lower and noted where we read them.

How does CloudRift compare to AWS, Azure and GCP on GPU pricing?

CloudRift sells the same V100 and L40S cards at $0.25 to $0.63 per GPU-hour against $1.86 to $3.06 at the hyperscalers, and consumer-class RTX cards they do not offer at all. It does not sell the H100, H200 or B200 on demand. Current availability per instance size is in the console.

How often is this page updated?

The provider columns were read on October 15, 2026 and are re-checked quarterly; the date is printed at the top of the page. The CloudRift column comes from our API on every rebuild and is at most five minutes old.

The console shows the same hourly rates as this page with current availability per instance size. Reserved terms for the cards above are quoted on request.

CloudRift Platform Update, October 2026: Agent Skills, Billing Rules, Saved Environments

# What's New in CloudRift: Agent Skills, Fairer Billing, and Saved Disks

Everything that shipped in versions 0.62 and 0.63, translated from the changelog

By Heiko Polinski• October 29, 2026

Product Updates GPU Rental Infrastructure

Engineering posts every CloudRift release in our Discord, and the changelog carries the full notes. Those notes are written for people who run the platform. This post is for everyone else. It covers what changed between early September and late October 2026, what it means if you rent GPUs, and what it means if you host them.

...

## You pay for a running VM, not for waiting

Two releases closed gaps in how rentals were charged. Since 0.62.0, the funds for a rental are held when you create it and charged once the VM is running. If the VM never starts, or the node stops responding, the hold is returned and you are not billed. Since 0.63.0, billing stops the moment you terminate, even if the node is still cleaning up behind the scenes. Reservation purchases and extensions now check your balance in the same transaction that charges, which fixed a race where two purchases in the same minute could overdraw an account.
